E-commerce Customer Behaviour Analysis · Findings Report

What Your Data Is Telling You About Your Customers

This report communicates key customer insights derived from an open-source E-commerce business dataset obtained from Kaggle. The dataset used is anonymized and analyzed at an aggregated level to protect individual privacy and prevent identification of specific customers. This report presents the outcomes of data analysis conducted to answer key business questions: why customers stop purchasing, whether there are early indicators of customer loss, how seasonal and time-based patterns influence churn probability, and how current customer retention strategies are performing. Written for decision makers. Prepared by Everlynn Muthoni.

Dataset Size10,000
Visualizations8 Charts
Key Variables15 Columns
Data Context Period2020 – 2024
Executive Summary

The Three Headlines Before You Read On

⚠
Churn (percentage of customers that ceased their relatioship with the business) is uniformly high and unexplained by behaviour. Across every segment, every lifecycle stage, every season, every purchase timing. Churn probability averages ~50%. This is the single most important finding and demands immediate attention and investigation.
◈
Revenue is flat and unchanging across lifecycle stages. New customers and loyal customers generate nearly identical lifetime value (~$4,900–$5,077). This challenges our assumption that loyalty drives revenue growth for this business, and may suggest a value ceiling problem, and not just a retention problem as was assumed.
◆
No single behavioural variable reliably predicts churn. Purchase frequency, purchase gaps, season, time of day, and adopter type (as provided in the data), none show meaningful correlation or causation with churn probability. Churn may be driven by factors not yet in this dataset.
"The data does not yet explain why customers leave. That is itself a finding, and it tells us exactly where to look next. Customer Experince Post Purchase"
Chart 01A

Are there Signals that Precede Churn?

"Does buying more frequently make a customer less likely to leave?"
Here we analysed Purchase Frequency vs Churn Risk · 10,000 customers · 4 product categories
Left Panel: How to interprete the visual Each coloured dot is one customer. Their position left to right shows how often they buy (Purchase Frequency). Up and down shows their churn risk. The gold dashed line is the overall trend. Notice it is almost perfectly horizontal This means that wheater a customer buys more or alot less products, the business stands equal chance of lossing them.
Right Panel: How to interprete the visual Each bar is the average churn probability for customers. Every single bar sits at roughly the same height (~0.50). Whether a customer buys 2 times or 19 times, their average churn risk is identical.Frequency of purchase is not a great predictor of loyalty or churn for the ecommerce business.
Red dotted line The horizontal red dotted line on the left at 0.70 marks the "high risk" threshold. Every group has customers above and below it, this confirms no frequency level is "safe".
What the data shows The statistical correlation between purchase frequency and churn probability is +0.018. This is essentially zero across 10,000 customers. The trend line is flat. Frequent buyers are no more loyal than the infrequent ones.
What this means for the business We are generating transactions, but not attachment. Customers who buy repeatedly are not bonding. They may be buying out of convenience, not loyalty. Is this in line with the business objectives?
Strategic action Do not use purchase frequency as an indicator for customer health. A "loyal" customer who buys 15 times is just as likely to leave as someone who bought twice. Churn risk is caused by something else entirely. Customer experince? the competitor landscape? further investigation is required.
Chart 01B

Could The Time Gap Between Purchases be a Churn Signal?

"Do customers who go quiet, with longer gaps between purchases, show higher churn risk?"
Here we analysed the Days Between Purchases split into Churn Risk Band: Low / Medium / High
How to interprete this chart Each coloured box represents a group: green = Low Risk customers, blue = Medium Risk, red = High Risk. The horizontal line through the middle of each box is the median, the typical gap. The box top and bottom show the range for most customers.
The critical observation All three boxes are nearly the same size, same position, same median. The typical gap between purchases is ~46 days for Low Risk, ~47 for Medium Risk, ~48 for High Risk. A difference of 1 to 2 days across 10,000 customers is statistically low.
This disapproves the assumption that; "Going quiet", taking longer between purchases, is a reliable early warning sign In this customer base. Standard recency-based churn models may not apply here. Churn may be more sudden and event-driven than gradual.
What the data shows Median purchase gap is 46d (Low Risk), 47d (Medium), 48d (High Risk). The three boxes overlap almost perfectly. Purchase gap does not differentiate churners from loyal customers.
What this means for the business Customers do not appear to be slowly fading before they leave. They may be leaving suddenly, after a specific bad experience, a competitor offer, or a price change, rather than through gradual disengagement.
Strategic action Invest in capturing why customers leave, not just when. Exit surveys, complaint logs, and service interaction data are more likely to predict churn here than purchase timing patterns.
Chart 02 ·

Does Timing Patterns affect Customer Loyalty?

"Morning, evening, Winter, Summer, does this predict how loyal customers are?"
On the Left: We analysed Season × Time of Day for churn risk · On the Right: We analysed Average Lifetime Value by time and retention strategy
Left Chart: How to interpret Each cell combines a season (rows) with a preferred purchase time (columns). The colour should ideally range from deep green (low churn) to deep red (high churn). Instead, every cell is the same pale yellow-green. All values sit between 0.488 and 0.524.
Right Chart: How to interpret The three coloured bars in each group show the average lifetime value, this is net revenue a business can expect from a single customer, under each retention strategy (Discount, Email Campaign, Loyalty Program). All bars reach the same height, approximately $5,000, across all three purchase time segments.
The Observation Timing has no observable effect on churn or LTV. Winter Afternoon shoppers (0.52) are not meaningfully different from Summer Evening shoppers (0.49). The 0.03 difference across 10,000 customers is not significant.
What the data shows All 12 season time combinations show churn between 0.49–0.52. All three retention strategies produce near-identical lifetime values (~$4,900–$5,100) across morning, afternoon, and evening shoppers.
What this means for the business Time or season based customer segmentation will not improve retention outcomes. Any deployed different strategies to morning vs evening shoppers, or to Winter vs Summer customers, have produced no measurable difference yet.
Strategic action Redirect the budget and effort spent on time-based targeting. More importantly: since all three retention strategies show identical outcomes, a controlled experiment is needed to test whether any of them are actually working, or whether a completely different approach is required.
Data Scientist's Note

The heatmap colour scale spans 0.30–0.75 but all data sits in the narrow 0.49–0.52 band. This makes the gradient appear more meaningful than it is. The real insight is the absence of variation Which is what makes this chart important.

Chart 03 ·

Does Revenue Change Across the Customer Lifecycle?

"Do customers who buy more often generate significantly more revenue?"
On the Left: We analysed Lifetime Value distribution per Customer lifecycle stage · On the Right: We analysed Mean Average Order Value and Lifetime Value per Customer lifecycle stage
Left chart: How to interpret Each violin shows the distribution of Lifetime Value for one customer group. The wider the shape at any dollar level, the more customers sit at that value. The three dashed lines inside mark the 25th percentile (lower), median (middle), and 75th percentile (upper). Compare the four violins, they should look different if customer lifecycle stage matters in this business.
What stands out All four violins are almost identical in shape and span. Each stretches from near $0 to $10,000+, with similar widths throughout. The median (middle dashed line) sits at roughly $5,000 in all four stages. The shape does not change as customers mature.
Right chart: How to interpret The gold bars (Customer Lifetime Value) are all the same height. The blue bars (Average Order Value) are all the same tiny height, approximately $110 per order, regardless of stage. The visual gap between them is real: AOV is low relative to LTV because LTV accumulates across many orders.
$4,935

$5,077
Developing LTV
$5,035

$5,047
Loyal LTV
What the data shows The LTV difference between a New customer ($4,935) and a Loyal customer ($5,047) is just $112, across four entire lifecycle stages. Average Order Value is equally flat at ~$110 per stage. Customer progression does not translate to very significant revenue growth.
What this means for the business The efforts of moving a customer from "New" to "Loyal" adds no significant incremental revenue per head. The business has the same revenue ceiling for a new customer as it does for its most frequent one. This is a growth architecture problem.
Strategic action Identify the top 20% of customers by actual LTV and analyse what differentiates them, are they buying across multiple categories? Higher AOV items? More recent acquisitions? The answer to "what creates value here?" is not frequency. It is something else in the data we haven't yet isolated.
"A loyal customer generating the same revenue as a new one is not a loyalty problem. It is a value capture problem."
Chart 04 ·

Does How Long The Products have existed, affect customer LTV?

"Does a longer relationship with the brand translate into more value over time?"
To the Left:We analysed Distribution of product age since launch date · To the Right: We analysed Product age vs Customer Lifetime Value with trend line
Left chart: How to interpret The blue bars show how many customers are associated with products of each age (in days since launch). The gold KDE curve traces the smooth overall shape. The distribution is relatively even from ~400 to ~1,400 days, with a peak around 1,000–1,100 days, then a natural fall-off for very recent products.
Right chart: How to interpret Each dot is a customer: positioned left to right by how old the product is, and up down by their lifetime value. If older products produced more valuable customers, dots on the right should sit higher. The red trend line shows what actually happens, it is almost perfectly flat across the entire range.
The takeaway The correlation between product age and LTV is −0.005, which is statistically very low. Time in the relationship, whether 1 year or 4 years, adds no additional value. The business is not compounding its relationship with customers over time.
What the data shows Products range from 365 to 1,461 days old. Despite a 4-year spread, customers associated with older products generate no more lifetime value than those with newer ones. The trend line is flat with correlation −0.005.
What this means for the business Tenure(how long a customer is with the business) is not being monetised. A customer of 4 years generates the same revenue as one of 1 year. This is consistent with the lifecycle chart: the business generates similar value from customers regardless of relationship length.
Strategic action Investigate whether long-tenure customers are buying the same single product repeatedly vs expanding into other categories. Breadth of relationship, not length, may be the true driver of high LTV. Adding a "number of distinct categories purchased" column to the dataset would confirm this quickly.
Chart 05 ·

Does Product Peak Performance produce more value?

"How long does it take a product to reach its best sales period, and do fast peaking products produce more valuable customers?"
To the Left: We analysed Distribution of days from launch to peak sales, by product category · To the Right: We analysed Days to peak vs customer Lifetime Value
Left Chart — Interpreting the histogram The overlapping coloured bars show, for each product category, how many products peaked at each day count after launch. The red dashed line marks the overall median (~730 days). A bell-shape peaking near that line means most products take about two years to reach their sales highpoint.
Category comparison All four categories, Electronics (pink), Clothing (gold), Sports (green), Home (teal), show similar bell-shaped distributions centred around 700–750 days. No category is dramatically faster or slower to peak than the others. The market treats all categories similarly.
Right chart: Interpreting Speed vs Value The scatter shows each customer plotted by their product's time to peak (horizontal) against their LTV (vertical). The coloured dots are evenly distributed across the full range with no upward or downward pattern. Confirming that fast peaks do not produce higher-value customers.

1,454

What the data shows Across all four categories, the median time from product launch to peak sales is approximately 725–740 days (~2 years). The distribution is roughly bell-shaped. Speed to peak has no relationship with customer lifetime value.
What this means for the business Product investment decisions should use a two-year horizon for performance assessment. Early spikes in a product's sales are not predictors of long-run customer quality or revenue. Slow-building products are not underperformers.
Strategic action Avoid making go/no-go decisions on products within the first 6–12 months. The data shows most products need ~2 years to reach their natural peak audience. Early results are poor proxies for long-run potential.
Chart 06 ·

Early Adopters vs Later Users, is there a difference in business value?

"Do customers who discovered our products early generate more value and show more loyalty than those who came later?"
Three panels: Lifetime Value · Average Order Value · Churn Risk: Comparing Early Adopters (gold) vs Later Users (blue)
Panel 1: Lifetime Value The two boxes (gold = Early Adopter, blue = Later User) show the distribution of total customer value. The median line through each box sits at approximately $5,000 for both groups. The boxes are the same height, same width, same range. Early adoption confers no LTV advantage.
Panel 2: Average Order Value Same story: gold and blue boxes sit at the same median (~$110 per order) with similar spreads from ~$50 to ~$200. Early adopters do not spend more per transaction than later arrivals.
Panel 3: Churn Risk violin Both violin shapes are wide and even, spreading from near 0 to 1.0 with mass distributed across the full churn probability range. The red dotted line at 0.70 (high-risk threshold) cuts through both equally. Neither group is safer from churn.
What the data shows Early Adopters: LTV $5,017 · AOV $109.75 · Churn 0.50. Later Users: LTV $5,061 · AOV $110.52 · Churn 0.50. The groups are statistically indistinguishable on all three measures.
What this means for the business Being first to discover a product does not make a customer more valuable, more loyal, or more likely to spend more. Early adoption is not rewarding itself through any measurable behaviour premium.
Strategic action Reconsider early adopter incentive programmes if their rationale is that early customers are inherently more valuable. The data does not support that. What may matter more is the quality of the post-acquisition experience, regardless of when that acquisition happened.
Chart 08 ·

What is the Churn Risk Across Customer Lifecycle Stages

"Does churn risk decrease as customers mature, and are Loyal customers genuinely safer?"
Stacked bars show % of customers in Low / Medium / High risk bands per lifecycle stage · White line = mean churn probability (right axis)
How to read the bars Each bar represents one lifecycle stage. Green at the bottom = Low Risk customers (churn prob below 0.33). Blue in the middle = Medium Risk (0.33–0.66). Red at the top = High Risk (above 0.66). A "good" business would show the green section growing as you move right toward Loyal customers.
What actually happens All four bars look almost identical. Each has roughly 33% green at the bottom, 33% blue in the middle, and 33% red at the top. The High Risk (red) band does not shrink as customers become more "Loyal". It stays the same, or very slightly grows (New: 32.8% high risk vs Loyal: 33.5%).
The white line The white line traces mean churn probability across stages (read on the right axis). It sits flat at 0.50–0.51 across all four stages, confirming the visual story in the bars: lifecycle advancement does not reduce churn probability. There is no safe harbour at the "Loyal" end.
What the data shows Churn risk is split almost perfectly into equal thirds (Low / Medium / High) at every lifecycle stage. The mean churn probability is 0.494 (New) vs 0.506 (Loyal), churn risk very marginally increases as customers advance. No stage is a safe zone.
What this means for the business The assumption "if we get customers to be Loyal, they will self-sustain" is not supported. A third of the most frequent buyers are in the high-risk band. Frequency of purchase and churn risk are independent of each other.
Strategic action Retention effort must be applied across the entire customer base, at every lifecycle stage, not concentrated on early-stage customers only, as earlier assumed. The business needs a churn intervention model that works on inputs other than purchase frequency, because frequency is not the driver.
"A customer buying 15 times a year who is still at 33% high-risk is not a loyal customer. They are a high-frequency, high-risk customer. Those require different solutions."
Summary · All 8 Analyses Together

The Pattern Behind Every Assumption

Stepping back across all eight charts, one conclusion dominates: this dataset reveals a business with a significant churn problem that is not yet explained by the behavioural variables available. That is a specific and important finding — not a failure of analysis.

Variable Tested What We Expected What the Data Shows Signal
Purchase Frequency vs ChurnHigher frequency = lower churnNo relationship (r = 0.018)⚑ Unexpected
Purchase Gap vs ChurnLonger gap = higher churnIdentical medians (~47 days)⚑ Unexpected
Season × Time vs ChurnWinter/Evening = higher riskUniform 0.49–0.52 across all— No signal
Lifecycle Stage vs LTVLoyal = highest LTVAll stages ~$5,000 (±$142)⚑ Unexpected
Product Age vs LTVLonger tenure = more valueNo relationship (r = −0.005)⚑ Unexpected
Days to Peak vs LTVFaster peak = higher value ceilingNo pattern across categories— No signal
Early Adopter vs Later UserEarly = more loyal, higher LTVIdentical on all three metrics— No signal
Lifecycle Stage vs Churn RiskLoyal stage = lowest churn~33% high risk in every stage⚑ Unexpected
The Honest Interpretation for My Client

Five of eight expected relationships are not supported by the data. This is not neessarily a problem. It is a signal that the variables currently captured may not be the primary drivers of churn in this business.


The next analytical step: ask what is not in this dataset that might explain the pattern. Strong candidates include: product return and complaint history, customer service interaction logs, price sensitivity signals, whether customers are single-product or multi-product buyers, and competitor activity. Churn that cannot be explained by transactional behaviour is typically driven by experience data.

Recommendations · What to Do Next

Three Concrete Next Steps

Recommendation 01 · Data Expansion

Capture the variables that may actually predict churn

Add to your dataset: last purchase date (true recency), number of distinct product categories purchased (breadth of relationship), return and complaint history, and customer service touchpoints. These "experience" variables are the typical drivers of churn when behavioural frequency variables are flat.

Recommendation 02 · Retention Strategy Experiment

Test whether any retention strategy is actually working

All three current strategies, Loyalty Program, Discount, Email Campaign, show identical lifetime value outcomes (~$5,000). This means either all three work equally well, or none are moving the needle. Design a 90-day controlled experiment with a no-intervention control group. Without a control baseline, the effectiveness of any strategy cannot be measured.

Recommendation 03 · Re-segment by Value, Not Behaviour

Replace frequency-based lifecycle tiers with value-based ones

Since lifecycle stage based on purchase frequency shows no meaningful revenue difference, replace it with value-based segmentation. Customers in the top 20% of LTV, regardless of how often they buy, represent your most defensible revenue. Understand who they are, what they buy differently, and why they stayed. That is where the insight this data is pointing toward actually lives.
